Gambles and expected value

Section titled “Gambles and expected value”

Investing, buying insurance and choosing a career are all decisions made when the outcome is uncertain. An uncertain outcome written as “each outcome and its probability”, like the scenario tables of 0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance, is called a gamble (lottery).

Is the expected value enough? Imagine you have 100,000 dollars and someone offers a gamble: flip a coin; heads you win 50,000 dollars, tails you lose 50,000 dollars. The expected gain is 0, but most people refuse. If heads wins 60,000 and tails loses 50,000, the expected gain is positive (5,000 dollars), and many people still refuse. So people look not only at the expected value; they also care about how much the outcome varies.

Expected utility

Section titled “Expected utility”

The standard approach in economics is to measure the satisfaction from wealth WWW with a utility function u(W)u(W)u(W) and then take the expectation of utility. The expected utility of a gamble is

E[u(W)]=∑ipi u(Wi)E[u(W)] = \sum_i p_i\,u(W_i)E[u(W)]=i∑​pi​u(Wi​)

People choose the option with the highest expected utility. Unlike in 1.2 Consumer Theory, the size of utility matters here: it is used to average the outcomes with weights. uuu allows only positive linear transformations a+b ua + b\,ua+bu (b>0b > 0b>0), not any increasing transformation; otherwise the ranking of gambles could change.

Someone's utility function is u(W)=Wu(W) = \sqrt{W}u(W)=W​ (WWW in thousand dollars). Gamble L leaves him with 64 or 16 with equal probability. Does he prefer L or 38 for sure? What are the certainty equivalent and the risk premium of L?

Risk aversion

Section titled “Risk aversion”

A person who always prefers receiving the expected value of a gamble for sure to taking the gamble shows risk aversion:

u(E[W])>E[u(W)]u\big(E[W]\big) > E\big[u(W)\big]u(E[W])>E[u(W)]

This inequality holds for all gambles exactly when uuu is strictly concave (u′′<0u'' < 0u′′<0): the more wealth one has, the less utility one more dollar adds. In the example above, losing 50,000 dollars lowers utility by more than winning 50,000 dollars raises it.

  • uuu is a straight line (u′′=0u'' = 0u′′=0): risk neutral, looking only at expected values;
  • uuu is convex (u′′>0u'' > 0u′′>0): risk loving.

The degree of risk aversion is measured by the Arrow–Pratt coefficients. The coefficient of absolute risk aversion and the coefficient of relative risk aversion are

A(W)=−u′′(W)u′(W),R(W)=−W u′′(W)u′(W)A(W) = -\frac{u''(W)}{u'(W)}, \qquad R(W) = -\frac{W\,u''(W)}{u'(W)}A(W)=−u′(W)u′′(W)​,R(W)=−u′(W)Wu′′(W)​

Dividing by u′u'u′ makes the coefficients unaffected by positive linear transformations of uuu. AAA measures the attitude to gambles of a fixed dollar size, and RRR the attitude to gambles proportional to wealth.

Check C2
For each utility function (W>0W > 0W>0), state whether it represents risk aversion, risk neutrality or risk loving: (a) u=W2u = W^2u=W2; (b) u=2W+3u = 2W + 3u=2W+3; (c) u=ln⁡Wu = \ln Wu=lnW. For (c), find the coefficients of absolute and relative risk aversion.

Certainty equivalent and risk premium

Section titled “Certainty equivalent and risk premium”

A sure amount that gives the same utility as the expected utility of a gamble is called the gamble’s certainty equivalent (CE):

u(CE)=E[u(W)]u(\text{CE}) = E\big[u(W)\big]u(CE)=E[u(W)]

The difference between the expected value and the certainty equivalent is called the risk premium: the expected wealth a person is willing to give up to remove the risk.

π=E[W]−CE\pi = E[W] - \text{CE}π=E[W]−CE

Example: u(W)=ln⁡Wu(W) = \ln Wu(W)=lnW, wealth 100 (thousand dollars), and a gamble that changes wealth to 150 or 50 with equal probability. E[W]=100E[W] = 100E[W]=100, and

E[ln⁡W]=12ln⁡150+12ln⁡50=ln⁡7500,CE=7500≈86.60E[\ln W] = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln 150 + \tfrac{1}{2}\ln 50 = \ln\sqrt{7500}, \qquad \text{CE} = \sqrt{7500} \approx 86.60E[lnW]=21​ln150+21​ln50=ln7500​,CE=7500​≈86.60

The risk premium is about 13.40: this person would rather have 86.6 for sure than take a gamble with an expected value of 100.

For small gambles there is an approximation for the risk premium (derived in Exercises Question 2):

π≈12 A(W) σ2\pi \approx \tfrac{1}{2}\,A(W)\,\sigma^2π≈21​A(W)σ2

where σ2\sigma^2σ2 is the variance of the gamble. The risk premium is proportional to the variance: doubling the risk (the standard deviation) makes the premium four times as large. In the example, A=1W=0.01A = \frac{1}{W} = 0.01A=W1​=0.01 and σ=50\sigma = 50σ=50, so the approximation gives 12×0.01×2500=12.5\frac{1}{2} \times 0.01 \times 2500 = 12.521​×0.01×2500=12.5, close to the exact 13.40; the larger the gamble, the less accurate the approximation.

Insurance

Section titled “Insurance”

Risk aversion explains why people are willing to pay more than the expected loss to buy insurance.

Example: a household has wealth of 100 (thousand dollars), of which its house is worth 75. Each year there is a 1% chance of a fire that destroys the house. The expected loss is 0.01×75=0.750.01 \times 75 = 0.750.01×75=0.75. With u=ln⁡Wu = \ln Wu=lnW and no insurance,

E[u]=0.99ln⁡100+0.01ln⁡25,CE=1000.99×250.01≈98.62E[u] = 0.99\ln 100 + 0.01\ln 25, \qquad \text{CE} = 100^{0.99} \times 25^{0.01} \approx 98.62E[u]=0.99ln100+0.01ln25,CE=1000.99×250.01≈98.62

With full insurance, wealth is 100−P100 - P100−P for sure, where PPP is the premium. Insurance is better as long as 100−P≥98.62100 - P \ge 98.62100−P≥98.62, that is, P≤1.38P \le 1.38P≤1.38. The highest premium this household would pay is about 1.38, nearly twice the expected loss.

Why is the insurer willing to bear the risk? It insures a large number of independent policies; by the reasoning of 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference, the average payout per policy is almost certain, so the insurer can be treated as roughly risk neutral. Any premium between 0.75 and 1.38 makes both sides better off than without insurance.

Check C4
Someone has wealth of 50 (thousand dollars), of which a car is worth 20. Within a year the car has a 5% chance of a total loss. u=ln⁡Wu = \ln Wu=lnW. What is the expected loss? What is the highest premium he would pay for full insurance?

CRRA utility

Section titled “CRRA utility”

The most common utility function in finance is

u(W)=W1−γ1−γ(γ>0, γ≠1),u(W)=ln⁡W(γ=1)u(W) = \frac{W^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma} \quad (\gamma > 0,\ \gamma \ne 1), \qquad u(W) = \ln W \quad (\gamma = 1)u(W)=1−γW1−γ​(γ>0, γ=1),u(W)=lnW(γ=1)

A calculation gives R(W)=γR(W) = \gammaR(W)=γ: the coefficient of relative risk aversion is constant, hence the name CRRA utility (constant relative risk aversion). The larger γ\gammaγ, the more risk averse; log utility is the special case γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1.

An important property of CRRA is that a person’s attitude toward a gamble in which “wealth rises or falls by some proportion” does not depend on how wealthy he is. In proportional terms, the approximation for the risk premium becomes

πW≈12 γ σ2\frac{\pi}{W} \approx \tfrac{1}{2}\,\gamma\,\sigma^2Wπ​≈21​γσ2

where σ\sigmaσ is the standard deviation of the percentage change in wealth. This property makes a CRRA investor put a fixed share of wealth into risky assets, however wealthy he is. 4.3 The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line (not yet published) uses it to derive the best share in stocks, and 4.12 Life-Cycle Asset Allocation Theory (not yet published) uses it to analyze asset allocation over a lifetime. Most estimates of γ\gammaγ in research lie between 1 and 10.

0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference showed that the expected value of wealth is pulled up by a few very good outcomes and that the median better represents a typical outcome. An investor with log utility maximizes E[ln⁡W]E[\ln W]E[lnW], that is, the expected log return, which is in line with caring about the median (Exercises Question 4).

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Expected utility: E[u(W)]=∑pi u(Wi)E[u(W)] = \sum p_i\,u(W_i)E[u(W)]=∑pi​u(Wi​); utility allows only positive linear transformations.
  • Risk aversion is equivalent to a concave uuu; its degree is measured by A=−u′′u′A = -\frac{u''}{u'}A=−u′u′′​ and R=−Wu′′u′R = -\frac{W u''}{u'}R=−u′Wu′′​.
  • The certainty equivalent satisfies u(CE)=E[u(W)]u(\text{CE}) = E[u(W)]u(CE)=E[u(W)]; the risk premium is π=E[W]−CE≈12Aσ2\pi = E[W] - \text{CE} \approx \frac{1}{2} A \sigma^2π=E[W]−CE≈21​Aσ2.
  • Risk-averse people are willing to pay premiums above the expected loss; an insurer with many independent risks is close to risk neutral.
  • CRRA utility has constant relative risk aversion γ\gammaγ, and the proportional risk premium is about 12γσ2\frac{1}{2}\gamma\sigma^221​γσ2.

(a) Expand E[u(W)]E[u(W)]E[u(W)] around μ\muμ to second order.
(b) Expand u(μ−π)u(\mu - \pi)u(μ−π) around μ\muμ to first order.
(c) From u(μ−π)=E[u(W)]u(\mu - \pi) = E[u(W)]u(μ−π)=E[u(W)], derive π≈12A(μ)σ2\pi \approx \frac{1}{2}A(\mu)\sigma^2π≈21​A(μ)σ2. Why is a first-order expansion enough in (b)?
Question 3

(a) Verify that the coefficient of relative risk aversion is R(W)=γR(W) = \gammaR(W)=γ.

Question 4 ★
Return to the coin-flip investment of 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference: each year, wealth is multiplied by 1.5 or 0.6 with equal probability, an expected growth of 5% a year. An investor with log utility (u=ln⁡Wu = \ln Wu=lnW) considers it.
(a) If he invests all his wealth, is E[ln⁡W]E[\ln W]E[lnW] after one year higher or lower than without investing? Would he invest everything?
(b) If he invests a share fff (holding the rest in cash with zero return), wealth is multiplied by 1+0.5f1 + 0.5f1+0.5f or 1−0.4f1 - 0.4f1−0.4f. Find the fff that maximizes E[ln⁡W]E[\ln W]E[lnW].
(c) Investing the fff from (b), by how much does E[ln⁡W]E[\ln W]E[lnW] rise each year? How does this relate to the "growth of median wealth" in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference?
Question 5
An insurer writes car policies like the one in Check C4: each policy pays 20 (thousand dollars) with probability 5% and 0 otherwise.
(a) What are the expected payout and the standard deviation of one policy?
(b) The insurer writes 10,000 independent policies. What is the standard deviation of the average payout per policy?
(c) The insurer charges a premium of 1.1 per policy. An average payout above 1.1 is about how many standard deviations above the mean? Why can the insurer be treated as roughly risk neutral?
(d) If all the cars are in the same city and the main risk is a single hailstorm, do the conclusions of (b) and (c) still hold?
Question 6
A client says that she finds "having 800,000 dollars for sure" as good as "having 500,000 or 1.5 million dollars with equal probability". Assume her utility is CRRA.
(a) About what is her coefficient of relative risk aversion γ\gammaγ? (You may solve with a calculator or code.)
(b) What is the certainty equivalent of this gamble for someone with log utility? Is she more or less risk averse than such a person?
